label: Psychology
title: Why We Judge Others So Quickly – The Fundamental Attribution Error
thumbnail_text: You judge them, not their day
description: When someone else makes a mistake, we see their character. When we make the same mistake, we see our circumstances. In this calm video essay we look at the 1967 Castro essay study by Edward Jones and Victor Harris, Lee Ross's naming of the fundamental attribution error in 1977, the quizmaster experiment, and a morning practice from Marcus Aurelius' Meditations – and at how a little charitable interpretation can make our judgments of other people more accurate.

sections.text:
Someone cuts in front of you in traffic. In the half second it takes to brake, you already know who they are. Careless. Selfish. The kind of person who thinks the rules are for everyone else.

Now imagine you are the one who cut in. You know exactly why. You were late, a child was crying in the back seat, you simply did not see the other car.

Same action. Two completely different explanations. One is about character. The other is about circumstances.

Psychologists have a name for this gap. And its story begins with a few short essays about Fidel Castro.

sections.heading: The Castro Essays
sections.text:
In 1967, the psychologists Edward Jones and Victor Harris ran a series of experiments with students at Duke University. The students read short essays about Fidel Castro's Cuba. Some essays were in favour of Castro, others against him.

Then came the twist. Some readers were told that the writer had freely chosen which side to take. Others were told that the writer had no choice: the position had been assigned by someone else, such as a course instructor or a debate coach.

The question for the readers was simple. What does the writer really think about Castro?

When the writer had chosen their side, it made sense to read the essay as their opinion. But what about the writers who had no choice? Logically, an assigned essay tells you very little about the person who wrote it.

And yet readers still judged the pro-Castro writers to be more in favour of Castro than the anti-Castro writers. The effect was smaller than when the writers had chosen freely, but it was clearly there. Even knowing about the situation, people read the words as a window into the person.

sections.heading: A Name for the Error
sections.text:
Ten years later, in 1977, the Stanford psychologist Lee Ross gave this pattern the name it is known by today: the fundamental attribution error.

Ross described it as our tendency to underestimate the power of situations, and to overestimate the role of personal traits, when we explain other people's behaviour. We see the action and assume it reveals the actor.

In the same year, Ross and his colleagues Teresa Amabile and Julia Steinmetz published a memorable demonstration. Students were randomly assigned to be either a quizmaster or a contestant. The quizmasters wrote their own difficult questions, drawn from whatever they happened to know. The contestants had to answer them.

Of course the contestants struggled. Anyone would, facing questions built around someone else's private knowledge. And yet afterwards, the quizmasters were rated as more knowledgeable than the contestants, even by the contestants themselves.

The roles had been handed out at random, but the advantage of the role was read as an advantage of the mind.

sections.heading: Why It Happens
sections.text:
Why do we do this? One reason is simply what we can see. When we watch someone else, the person is in the foreground: their face, their words, their action. The situation that shaped them, the pressure, the tiredness, the history, is mostly invisible.

When we explain our own behaviour, it is often the other way round. We cannot see ourselves from the outside, but we see everything around us very clearly. So we tend to explain our own mistakes by circumstances, and other people's mistakes by character. In 1971, Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett described this difference between how we see ourselves as actors and how we see others as observers. Same behaviour, different seat in the audience.

There may also be a kind of comfort in it. If people simply are what they do, the world feels more predictable. A bad driver is a bad person, and we are not like them.

Later research has added nuance. Some studies suggest the pattern is weaker in cultures that pay more attention to context and relationships, and it is not equally strong in every situation. But in everyday life, the first quick judgment often lands on the person, not on the circumstances.

sections.heading: The Emperor's Morning

quote.lead: Almost two thousand years ago, a Roman emperor prepared himself for exactly this. In the private notes we now call the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius wrote:
quote.text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations II.1, trans. George Long (1862)

sections.text:
At first this sounds rather grim. An emperor expecting the worst of everyone.

But read on, and the passage turns. Marcus does not conclude that these people are simply bad. He sees them as acting out of ignorance, and as his kin, sharing the same nature. He cannot be angry with his kinsman, he writes, nor hate him. In his words: we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth.

Marcus did not have the language of modern psychology. But he had noticed the same trap. When someone wrongs us, we leap to their character and stay there. His practice was to step back and see the wider picture: what led this person here, and how am I like them?

It is not an excuse for harm. Marcus still acted, still judged, still governed an empire. But he tried to judge actions without turning every action into a verdict on a whole person.

sections.heading: Charitable Interpretation
sections.text:
So what can we do with this? Philosophers speak of a principle of charity: when we interpret what someone says or does, we start from the most reasonable version, not the weakest.

In daily life it can be as simple as one extra question. When someone is short with you, or late, or careless, ask: what would have to be true for a decent person to act like this? Often the answers come quickly. They are tired. They are worried. They have just had bad news. They misunderstood.

You do not have to know which answer is right. The point is only to keep more than one explanation open for a moment longer. That moment is often enough to change the tone of what you say next.

Another habit is to borrow your own excuses. When you catch yourself judging someone, ask how you would explain the same behaviour if it were yours. Usually, you would reach for the situation first.

This is not about being naive. Some people do behave badly, and some patterns are real. But a single moment is rarely enough to know who someone is.

sections.heading: The Rest of the Story
sections.text:
Every person we meet is in the middle of a story we mostly cannot see. We see one scene, sometimes one second, and we are tempted to write the whole book from it.

The fundamental attribution error is not a moral failing. It is a shortcut of perception, and everyone takes it. The students reading the Castro essays were not unkind. They were simply doing what minds do: finding a person behind the words.

But we can learn to hold that first judgment a little more loosely. To remember that the driver who cut us off may be somebody's exhausted parent, or someone rushing to a hospital, or simply someone who did not see us.

And it may help to remember that others are doing the same to us. They see our worst second, and know nothing of our day.

A little generosity in how we read each other does not make the world less real. Very often, it makes our picture of it more accurate.

short.title: Why we judge others more harshly than ourselves
short.hook: Same mistake. Two very different verdicts.
short.text:
In 1967, students read essays about Fidel Castro. Some were told the writer had chosen their side. Others were told the side had been assigned.

Logically, an assigned essay says little about the writer. Yet readers still judged the pro-Castro writers to be more in favour of Castro.

In 1977, the psychologist Lee Ross named this the fundamental attribution error: when we explain other people, we overestimate character and underestimate circumstances.

When we make a mistake, we see the situation. When others do, we see the person.

So next time someone is short with you, ask: what would have to be true for a decent person to act like this?
